Discrete Bayesian Additive Regression Trees Sampler Data

dbartsData.Rd

Convenience function to create a data object for use with a dbarts sampler.

Usage

dbartsData(
    formula, data, test, subset, weights,
    offset, offset.test = offset,
    factors = c("categorical", "indicators"),
    na.action = dbarts::na.keepPredictors,
    counts = NULL, n.cuts = NULL, useQuantiles = NULL,
    keep.data = TRUE)

Arguments

formula, data, test, subset, weights, offset, offset.test, factors, na.action

As in dbarts. Retains backwards compatibility with bart, so that formula/data can be a formula/data.frame pair, or a pair of x.train/y.train matrices/vector. offset/offset.test take the matrix interface's shape from whether counts is also supplied: with counts, an n x K (nTest x K) numeric matrix installs the per-category shift described under counts below, and a flat vector is refused; without counts, only a flat vector (or single number) is accepted, and a matrix is refused. formula may itself be a dbartsData object, in which case it is returned as-is; any other argument supplied alongside it is then ignored, with a warning naming each one. weights are held as given, validated here only for length, NA and non-negativity; the family's own rule applies when a sampler is built from the object, where a "probit", "ordinal" or "nbinom" fit accepts only weights of 0 and 1, which name the rows in the data set and compose with the sampler's active-row mask.

n.cuts, useQuantiles

The maximum number of cut points per predictor, one number for every column, one per column, or by column or term name with .default for the rest, as bart's n.cuts reads, and whether to place them at the predictors' quantiles, which the data object then states; see dbarts. NULL, the default, states none. A count is kept as written and read again by the sampler it goes to, over the predictors that sampler holds: handed to a hazard sampler's $setData or to new("dbartsSampler", ...) with a person-period matrix, n.cuts = 7 gives the predictors 7 and the appended period column 100, as dbarts(n.cuts = 7, family = "hazard") does, and period takes a count only by its own name. A count one value short, or by name without period, is kept so a hazard sampler can read it, and any other sampler refuses it when it reads it; dbartsData itself refuses a count no sampler could read. Ignored, with the warning the other arguments draw, when formula is already a data object.

keep.data

Whether an object built from a formula and a data frame or list keeps the frame. TRUE, the default, keeps the frame as given, unless the build draws random numbers (see ‘Data kept’), the positions of the rows kept and what it takes to read the model's variables from them again, and holds no predictors, response, weights or offset: see ‘Data kept’. FALSE keeps the model matrix, the response, the weights and the offset in the object, as it was in 0.9-34, and no frame. An object built from an environment, with no data, or from the matrix interface keeps its matrix either way. formula being a dbartsData object takes the argument quietly.

counts

Optional n x K matrix of non-negative integer counts selecting the multinomial (softmax) model, column k holding category k's successes. A row may carry no trial: it enters no likelihood and still receives fitted probabilities. A row's trials, its count total, may not exceed \(10^6\), as each trial costs a Polya-Gamma draw per category per sweep. A row with any NA cell is a missing response, routed through na.action exactly as for every other family (see na.keepPredictors). It is restricted by subset exactly as weights is, and it IS the response: y is derived as its row sums - the trials \(n_i\) - so no separate response need be supplied, and any that is supplied is replaced. At least two categories are required. Column names, when present, label the categories. dbarts(family = "multinomial") writes this argument from a count-matrix or factor response rather than requiring it here. Under family = binomial or "logistic" an n x 2 matrix is instead the binomial response, its columns a row's successes and failures: y is again the row sums, the trials, and the offset is the flat shift on the log-odds a binary logistic fit takes; bart and dbarts write it from a cbind(successes, failures) response. Paired with counts, a matrix offset/offset.test is the per-category shift added to the raw per-category values BEFORE the softmax - which is the only place a shift means anything under one, since the blend is invariant to a common per-observation shift and a flat shift would be added after it. Only the row-centered part is identified: adding a constant to a whole row leaves every reported probability unchanged.

Details

Data kept

Built from a formula and a data frame or list, with keep.data = TRUE, the object keeps data whole (in its frame slot), rows, the positions in it of the rows kept after subset and the na.action, read from the model frame as lm reads them, so an na.action that records nothing of what it drops keeps the rows it returns (NULL when every row is kept in order; a repeated row, and a NA in subset that the na.action keeps, appear as they are), rows.total, the number of rows handed over, which rows are positions within (NULL where rows is), frame.columns, the names of its columns, frame.source, "frame" ("environment" beside the names of an environment the data were read from, and NULL where no data were given), and what reads the formula, weights and offset against the frame again. A caller's variable the formula, weights or offset names is kept as its value at the build, a function of no package among them, with the names it reads, so that a later change to the workspace, a function redefined or removed included, leaves the object unchanged; a function local to a caller's function is kept without the rest of that function's variables, and a package's function by name. A later change to data leaves the object unchanged. The slots x, y, and where they were given weights and offset hold a stand-in that stops, naming model.frame(object), under dim, length, [, as.matrix, as.numeric, arithmetic, sum, mean, c, rep, unique, cbind, rbind and sd; is.na, anyNA and is.finite stop too, rather than answer for values the slot does not hold; var and paste read it in R's own code, which gives no way to stop them, and answer NA with a warning or the slot's name; attr() of one gives NULL, and a weights or offset that was not given is NULL. Read the data with model.frame(object) and nobs(object). Every refusal and warning of the build is given at the build.

A sampler, and dbartsSpec's data, are made from the block-holding object that keep.data = FALSE gives, which the fitting functions make from a frame-keeping one by evaluating the formula against the frame again, on the kept rows, with the caller's variables as they were at the build; the sampler's data hold no frame. A frame-keeping object loaded in another session does this at its first fit, so the packages its formula calls must be installed there. A build whose formula, weights or offset draw from R's random-number generator, as rnorm(n) ~ x and y ~ jitter(x) do, keeps no frame and holds the values drawn, as keep.data = FALSE does, so that every fit from the object fits the same values; drawing data or subset does not count, as the frame and the rows are kept. A term drawing from a generator outside R's, which leaves R's stream where it was, is not seen: the object keeps its frame and draws again at each fit.

Data frame ingestion

Data frame columns - through the formula interface or a frame passed as x.train - map to predictors as follows:

  • numeric and logical columns enter as ordinal predictors, as do classed numbers such as Date, POSIXct and difftime, by their numeric value (a POSIXlt column is refused; convert it with as.POSIXct);

  • unordered factors each become a single categorical predictor under the default factors = "categorical", with splits sending a subset of levels down each branch; factors = "indicators" instead expands each factor into binary indicator columns, as previous versions always did - a factor past 100 levels builds this expansion as a sparse (dgCMatrix-backed) block automatically, with no user-facing argument: the tree structure grown is the same as the dense expansion's, though leaf-mean draws can differ from it in the last bit;

  • ordered factors enter as their own predictor kind, coded numerically by level order and split at a threshold on those codes; the split grid is the midpoints between consecutive declared levels, one candidate per level boundary, so n.cuts does not apply to such a column and adjacent levels are always separable;

  • matrix columns (e.g. from poly) splice in as ordinal predictors, one per column;

  • Matrix::sparseVector and dgCMatrix columns (assigned into the frame; they do not survive data.frame(...) or I()) enter as sparse ordinal predictors. Both interfaces accept them for training: a bare S4 column does not survive model.frame, so the formula path lifts any such column out of data before model.frame runs and re-attaches it, row-subset under subset and na.action alike, to the assembled predictor matrix afterward - named in formula like any other column, including through ., with no marker. A sparse name wrapped in poly(), ns(), log(), offset(), or a ':'/'*' interaction is refused by name, as an interaction among dense terms already is. test/x.test accepts them under either interface, since a test set is never run through model.frame;

  • sparseFactor columns enter as a single sparse categorical predictor, coded and binned identically to a dense factor of the same values. Both interfaces accept them, the same pull-out/re-attach the other sparse column kinds get on the formula path.

On the formula path, a sparse column re-attaches after every dense term regardless of where it was named, each in the order its name appears in formula (after . expansion) rather than its position in data; test is matched to x.train by name (or by position when neither carries names), so the two stay aligned regardless of this reordering. Factor level tables are retained so that test data are coded identically, and a factor predictor's level count - ordered or unordered - is the declared level table rather than the levels the training rows happen to take. A level declared but unobserved in training therefore keeps its own bin, and test or replacement data carrying it are accepted at every entrance (creation, setTestPredictor, predict, setPredictor, setData, which reads a factor of the new data by label against the sampler's table whatever levels it declares); conversely a value that is not an existing integer level code is refused at those same entrances, naming the kind, for ordered and unordered factors alike. An unordered factor is limited to 65535 levels and an ordered one to 65534 - one lower, since an ordered factor spends a code on the upper bin of its \(K - 1\) cut grid - and a wider one is an error naming the column. This holds equally for dense factors, sparseFactor columns, and dense factors inside a mixed dense/sparse frame. Drop unused levels before fitting (droplevels) if you would rather they not be modeled. test accepts the same column types as x.train, including sparseFactor and sparse ordinal columns. A sparseFactor or sparse ordinal test column recodes over the training level table and stays resident - through creation and setTestPredictor - rather than densifying at ingestion, the same storage tier rule as training. predict and getTrees(newdata = ) code a test set the same way and then route its rows through the trees off that storage, materializing no dense matrix of their own.

Data frame input is stored columnar: no \(n \times p\) double matrix is retained. Code that previously reached into the data object's x slot expecting a plain matrix should call extract(sampler, "predictors") - or as.matrix on the slot - to obtain the numeric predictor matrix, factor columns as their integer codes.

Value

An object of class dbartsData. Its frame, rows, frame.columns and frame.source slots are described under ‘Data kept’. Its rowNames slot records the names of the kept training and test rows, as list(train, test), or NULL when neither is named; a fit carries them on its outputs as the row names paragraph of bart's ‘Value’ section describes. Its bases, basis.levels, basis.written and basis.scale slots are NULL as created: a forest's basis is stated on the forest (see forest), and these slots are written on the data object a sampler of several forests holds. There bases holds each forest's block as the sampler uses it, a factor's level indicators among them; basis.levels records, for each forest of levels, the levels in the order of the block's columns, and NULL for a forest of numbers or with no basis; and basis.written the text each basis written as code was written as, NA for a basis handed over as a value and for a forest with none, by which a forest beside these data keeps the held basis (forest(basis = factor(z)) for one written factor(z)). on the data object a sampler holds it records, for each forest of numbers that states no sd, the standard deviation of its column over the rows in the likelihood when the sampler was first created, which that forest's default sd was taken from (see sd in forest), and a sampler created from such an object is handed it, so a copy, a reload and a sampler made again from its own control, model and data have the creation's prior whatever column is then in force. A forest that names a held basis by its text keeps the entry, wherever it stands in the list, and one given a new value takes the scale of that value; clearing an entry by hand has the next creation take the scale of the column in force. Its missing.seen slot is NULL as created; on the data object a sampler holds it records, once a predictor has been changed, the columns that sampler can hold missing values in, as a logical per predictor column (see ‘Missing values in predictors’ in dbartsSampler), and a sampler created from such an object takes them. Its status slot is NULL as created; on the data object an aft sampler holds it records the censoring status in force, 1 for an event and 0 for a censored row, which setResponse(status = ) rewrites and a copy or a reload is created from. Its useQuantiles slot is NA as created; on the data object a sampler holds it records whether the cut points are placed at the predictors' quantiles (see useQuantiles in dbartsControl), the value the sampler's control then carries.

Four more slots record what a sampler derives from its data; where basis.scale keeps the value of the sampler's first creation, they follow what the sampler holds while the data move. Each is NULL as created: cutPoints, a list with one entry per predictor column, NULL for an unordered factor and otherwise the column's cut points, strictly increasing, with their weights, where they are not equally likely, as the entry's "mass" attribute (an increasing sequence whose successive differences are the weights, as a state's cutMass holds them); response.range, the c(min, max) of the response the leaf prior's scale is taken from, NULL under a family that reads none (probit, logistic, ordinal and multinomial), and under nbinom c(center, center + 1) of the count fit's center, where a pair of another width, as a range recorded under another family is, is read by its first number, the sampler recording it as c(center, center + 1), and an equal pair is refused; forest.calibration, c(anchor = , unit = ) of a model of several forests (see forest), NULL elsewhere; and standardization, for a forest of linear or gp leaves a list with one entry per forest holding list(center = , scale = ), each named by the leaf covariates where each one's column name is present, non-empty and the name of no other column, and otherwise with columns, their column positions, beside them, a scale of NA for a covariate without spread, and beside them, for gp leaves whose model gives no lengthscale, the lengthscale derived with them; NULL as a whole, and not an entry per forest, where no forest's leaves take a covariate. The data object a sampler holds, sampler$data, records them from creation on, and the sampler rewrites them after every call that changes one. A sampler created from a data object - by dbarts, bart, dbartsSpec or new("dbartsSampler", control, model, data), and the copy and reload of a sampler, which are created from its own - uses each value the object records and derives the others, so dbarts(sampler$data) is made on the sampler's cut points, response range and leaf standardization, while a data object made afresh from the same rows derives its own. A sampler's setData does the same unless its updateCutPoints, updateScale or updateStandardization says to derive a value or to keep the sampler's (see dbartsSampler-class), so sampler$setData(sampler$data), the object handed back whole, keeps them. xbart takes cutPoints for every fold and derives the others in each fold, from the fold's training rows, whatever the object records. A record that fits no data - another number of columns, cut points for an unordered factor, on an ordered factor other than those of its levels, repeated or not finite, a range that is not two finite numbers, a standardization whose centers are not finite, whose scales are neither positive nor NA, whose lengthscales are not positive, whose names are missing, empty or repeated, or whose columns are not one position per center - is refused, naming the slot; setting it to NULL derives the value instead. Cut points out of order are sorted. Which covariates the leaves take is the model's, so a standardization is matched to them by its keys, names to leaf columns whose names could key one, the others deriving, columns where a leaf column's name could not, and one with neither by position where the counts agree: an entry for a covariate the leaves do not take is not read, a covariate without one is derived, and a lengthscale the model supplies is used in place of the record's.

See also

dbarts, model.frame.dbartsData, extract.dbartsSampler, sparseFactor

Examples

set.seed(3)
n <- 60L
df <- data.frame(
  x = runif(n),
  g = factor(sample(c("a", "b", "c"), n, replace = TRUE))
)
df$y <- df$x + 0.5 * (df$g == "b") + rnorm(n, 0, 0.1)

## the formula interface; 'g' enters as one categorical predictor
data <- dbartsData(y ~ x + g, df)
data

## the same data through the backwards-compatible x/y interface, with a
## test set that is coded against the training level table
train <- df[1:40, ]
test  <- df[41:60, c("x", "g")]
data <- dbartsData(train[, c("x", "g")], train$y, test)

## build a sampler on it, rather than letting dbarts() ingest again
sampler <- dbarts(data, control = dbartsControl(
  n.chains = 1L, n.threads = 1L, n.samples = 10L, n.burn = 10L,
  updateState = FALSE), n.trees = 25L)
samples <- sampler$run()
str(samples$test)
#>  num [1:20, 1:10] 0.283 0.78 0.663 0.536 0.478 ...
